extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent prosecutors and attorneys preparing or litigating patent claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and drafting patent claim language for definiteness under 35 U.S.C. § 112 (second paragraph) including terms of degree, subjective terms, numerical ranges, antecedent basis, functional and alternative limitations. Focuses on how examiners should analyze ambiguity and what applicants can do to remedy it.

rubrics_metrics.name: "About"
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining the range encompassed by the term “about”, one must consider the context of the term as it is used in the specification and claims of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze surrounding disclosure and prosecution history to determine what range "about" covers; note cases (Ortho-McNeil Pharm. v. Caraco; W.L. Gore v. Garlock) where "about" was definite (e.g., measurable with a stopwatch) and cases (Amgen v. Chugai) where "at least about" was indefinite because neither specification nor prior art indicated the covered range.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Essentially"
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase such as “a silicon dioxide source that is essentially free of alkali metal” can be definite if the specification contains guidelines and examples sufficient to enable a person of ordinary skill to draw the line between unavoidable impurities and essential ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for general guidelines and examples in the specification that teach where to draw the boundary; courts have held such phrasing definite where guidance exists (In re Marosi). Recognize that requiring a precise numeric cutoff may be impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Similar" / "Similar structure"
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the word “similar” (e.g., “nozzle for high-pressure cleaning units or similar apparatus”) can render a claim indefinite if it is not clear what applicant intended to cover by “similar.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If "similar" appears, determine whether the specification or prosecution history clarifies the meaning; absent clarification, examples show claims invalid (Ex parte Kristensen; Ex parte Pappas).

rubrics_metrics.name: "Substantially"
rubrics_metrics.description: The term “substantially” is a broad term often used with another term to describe a characteristic of the claimed invention; it may be definite when read in view of general guidelines in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the specification provides general guidelines or examples so that a person of ordinary skill would know what is meant (e.g., “substantially equal” held definite in Andrew Corp. v. Gabriel Electronics).

rubrics_metrics.name: "Type"
rubrics_metrics.description: The addition of the word “type” to an otherwise definite expression (e.g., “ZSM-5-type aluminosilicate zeolites”) can extend scope and render the claim indefinite if it is unclear what “type” was intended to convey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the dependent claims or specification place the recited "type" within the genus; unclear use of "type" has been held indefinite (Ex parte Copenhaver; Ex parte Attig).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other vague/relative terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like “relatively shallow,” “of the order of,” “substantial portion,” “or like material,” “comparable,” and “superior” have been held indefinite where the specification lacks a standard for measuring degree or comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the specification provides a standard or measurement method. Examples (Ex parte Oetiker; Ex parte Caldwell; Ex parte Anderson) show these terms are indefinite when no guidance exists as to degree, similarity, or which properties are to be compared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When a subjective term is used in the claim, the examiner should determine whether the specification supplies some standard for measuring the scope of the term; a claim that requires unrestrained subjective judgment may be indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess if intrinsic evidence provides objective standards; Datamize ("aesthetically pleasing") shows claims can be indefinite if meaning depends solely on individual opinion. During prosecution applicant may supply evidence that the term is ascertainable or amend to remove it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow and broader numerical ranges in the same claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a narrow numerical range that falls within a broader range in the same claim may render the claim indefinite when the boundaries of the claim are not discernible (e.g., including examples/preferences in a single claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unclear whether the narrower range is a limitation, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph. Examples: “a temperature of between 45 and 78 degrees Celsius, preferably between 50 and 60 degrees Celsius” or “a predetermined quantity, for example, the maximum capacity.” Dependent claims may properly set narrower ranges without indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-ended numerical ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Open-ended numerical ranges should be carefully analyzed for definiteness because they can create ambiguity in context (e.g., “at least 20% sodium” with dependent claims summing to 100% can create ambiguity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the open-ended wording creates contradictions with dependent claim language or percentages. Note that theoretical impossibilities (e.g., combined ranges summing to >100%) are not per se indefinite because impossible compositions cannot anticipate or infringe (In re Kroekel).

rubrics_metrics.name: "Effective amount"
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase “an effective amount” may or may not be indefinite; the proper test is whether one skilled in the art could determine specific values for the amount based on the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for disclosure (examples/guidelines) enabling determination of effective amounts (In re Mattison; In re Halleck). If the claim does not state the function to be achieved or multiple effects are implied, the phrase may be indefinite (In re Fredericksen). Recent cases accept "effective amount" when read in light of supporting disclosure and absence of prior-art uncertainty (Ex parte Skuballa).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary claim language ("for example", "such as")
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of examples or preferences is properly set forth in the specification rather than the claims. If stated in the claims, examples and preferences may lead to confusion over the intended scope of a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where it is not clear whether an example is limiting, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph. Provided examples held indefinite include: (A) “R is halogen, for example, chlorine”; (B) “material such as rock wool or asbestos”; (C) “lighter hydrocarbons, such, for example, as the vapors or gas produced”; (D) “normal operating conditions such as while in the container of a proportioner.” These are fact-specific and not per se rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is indefinite when it contains words or phrases whose meaning is unclear because there is no earlier recitation providing antecedent basis (e.g., referencing “said lever” where no lever was previously recited or two levers create ambiguity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for proper antecedent introductions. However, absence of explicit antecedent basis does not always render a claim indefinite if the scope is reasonably ascertainable to skilled artisans. Inherent components can supply antecedent basis (Energizer v. ITC; Ex parte Porter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner should suggest corrections to antecedent problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Antecedent problems are typically drafting oversights that are easily corrected once brought to the applicant's attention; the examiner should identify and suggest corrections constructively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address minor semantic drafting issues positively and constructively so major effort is spent on substantive issues. Indefiniteness is not excused merely because it could have been corrected (In re Hammack).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim term with no antecedent basis in the disclosure is not necessarily indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that a term used in the claim has no antecedent basis in the specification does not necessarily mean it is indefinite; words in the claim need not match the specification exactly so long as the claim defines the invention with reasonable clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim, read as a whole, apprises one of ordinary skill in the art of its scope; if so, it meets the notice function even without literal antecedent wording (In re Larsen example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim body reciting additional elements not per se indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is not per se indefinite if the body of the claim recites additional elements which do not appear in the preamble; consider the totality of limitations to ascertain scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the entire claim in context; courts have reversed rejections where the totality of limitations apprised skilled artisans of the scope (In re Larsen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to limitations in another claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim which makes reference to a preceding claim to define a limitation (e.g., “The product produced by the method of claim 1.”) is acceptable and should not necessarily be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such references are normally proper (Ex parte Porter). Only reject if the format of reference results in confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim term is functional when it recites a feature “by what it does rather than by what it is.” Functional language is not inherently improper and may be authorized (including means-plus-function under 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph), but must be evaluated for definiteness and written description/enablement support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate functional limitations in context of the specification and knowledge of a person of ordinary skill. Consider whether the limitation: (1) gives a clear-cut indication of scope; (2) sets well-defined boundaries or merely states a problem/result; and (3) would allow a skilled artisan to know what structure or steps are encompassed. Examples: some functional recitations accepted (In re Barr; In re Venezia), others rejected when they lack structure (Ariad; Hyatt). Examiner remedies: require quantitative metric, request formula/examples, show specification provides guidelines/examples, or require amendment to recite structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for examining functional language
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim limitation employs functional language, the examiner’s determination of whether the limitation is sufficiently definite will be highly dependent on context (disclosure and knowledge of a person of ordinary skill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider facts such as whether the limitation sets definite boundaries or merely describes a problem/result (Halliburton Energy Servs.), whether structural characteristics are adequately defined (General Elec.; United Carbon), and whether the specification provides general guidelines and examples (In re Marosi). Use these as non-exclusive points for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative limitations — Markush groups
rubrics_metrics.description: A “Markush” claim recites a list of alternatively useable species (commonly “selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C”). Markush claims are permissible if they present no uncertainty about scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure members of a Markush group belong to a recognized physical/chemical or art-recognized class, or at least share a common property responsible for their function. A Markush group may be indefinite if so expansive that skilled artisans cannot determine the metes and bounds. Double inclusion is not per se problematic; evaluate facts in each case. See MPEP §§ 803, 608.01(p), 715.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Or" terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative expressions using “or” (e.g., “wherein R is A, B, C, or D”) are acceptable and not per se in violation of 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases such as “made entirely or in part of,” “at least one piece,” and “iron, steel or any other magnetic material” have been held acceptable (In re Gaubert).

rubrics_metrics.name: "Optionally"
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the term “optionally” (e.g., “containing A, B, and optionally C”) can be acceptable where there is no ambiguity as to which alternatives are covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the list of potential alternatives can vary such that ambiguity arises, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph is proper; Ex parte Cordova and Ex parte Wu found such wording acceptable where unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative limitations (defining what a claim element is not) are not inherently ambiguous so long as the boundaries of the patent protection sought are set forth definitely, albeit negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the negative limitation provides definite boundaries; older cases criticized negative claiming that only excluded what was not invented (In re Schechter). If a negative limitation attempts to claim by exclusion without distinctly pointing out what was invented, it can be indefinite.
